name: h3
why: Uber's hexagonal geospatial index; a clever tiling system you can poke at for geometry and mapping.

brief.what_it_is: H3 is an open-source C library, developed at Uber, that indexes latitude/longitude points into a hexagonal grid. You give it a coordinate and a resolution from 0 to 15, and it returns a cell ID, a 64-bit index shown as a hex string. Given a cell ID, it can return the cell's hexagon boundary vertices or its center coordinate. The homepage describes it as a discrete global grid system, and the README says it is a hexagonal grid that can be approximately subdivided into finer hexagonal grids.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says H3 exists so that data can be joined across disparate datasets and aggregated at different levels of precision, and that the grid enables algorithms such as nearest neighbors, shortest path, and gradient smoothing. The README frames it as combining the benefits of a hexagonal grid with the hierarchical subdivisions of Google's S2 library.
brief.how_it_works: Each point is mapped to a cell at a chosen resolution, and each cell ID encodes its place in the hierarchy. The README says the hexagons can be approximately subdivided into finer hexagons, so cells nest across resolutions, though not perfectly. The command-line tools wrap the C API: latLngToCell takes coordinates and a resolution, and cellToBoundary and cellToLatLng take a cell index. The README does not explain the underlying projection or the indexing math beyond this.

brief.install_notes: On macOS, brew install h3 is the recommended route. The README says prebuilt bindings are preferred for other languages (Java, JavaScript, Python, and others), and that building from source needs a C compiler (gcc or clang tested), CMake, and Make. Windows builds need Visual Studio and CMake, following a separate build guide in the dev-docs folder. Installed binaries live under bin/ in the build tree, and the README's example commands use that path. Installing with make install puts them on the system path. No accounts or API keys are mentioned.
brief.standout: It is a hexagonal grid with a hierarchy, which is unusual because hexagons do not tile neatly across scales, and H3 accepts that the subdivision is only approximate. It also ships a small set of command-line tools that let you poke at cells straight from a shell.
brief.status: The README shows active CI badges for Linux, macOS, Windows, and the website, plus a coverage badge, and it links to a documentation site and a StackOverflow tag. I did not see a release date or last-commit date in what I fetched, so recent activity is not confirmed. Overall it looks maintained, but that is an inference from the badges and docs, not a dated fact.
brief.caveats: The README says nothing about Windows-only command-line tools, so the bin/ examples assume a Unix-like build. Building from source needs CMake and a C compiler, and contributors also need clang-format. Coverage reports need lcov and a Debug build with ENABLE_COVERAGE=ON. The brew metadata lists executables such as cellToBoundaryHier, cellToLatLngHier, cellToLocalIj, gridDisk, gridDiskUnsafe, h3ToComponents, h3ToHier, and localIjToCell, but the README does not show or explain them, so I did not verify them. The homepage is thin and mostly marketing copy. The repo includes DGGRID code credited to Southern Oregon University under the Apache 2.0 license. Contributions require signing Uber's CLA.

judge.reason: H3’s global hexagonal grid and approximate hierarchy open an interesting door into geospatial indexing, and it’s far from a familiar default for most developers.

entry.title: h3
entry.tldr: Uber's hexagonal geospatial index: turn a latitude and longitude into a short hex cell ID, then ask for that hexagon's corners or center.
entry.deeper_look:
H3 is a C library that divides the globe into hexagons. You give it a coordinate and a resolution from 0 (coarsest) to 15 (finest), and it returns a 64-bit cell ID, written as a hex string like `8a2a1072b59ffff`. Given a cell ID, it can hand back the hexagon's boundary vertices or its center point.

It was built at Uber so data from different sources could be joined on a shared grid and aggregated at different levels of precision. The homepage says the grid enables algorithms such as nearest neighbors, shortest path, and gradient smoothing. The README describes it as combining the benefits of a hexagonal grid with the hierarchical subdivisions of Google's S2 library.

The idea underneath is the awkward part. Hexagons do not nest neatly inside bigger hexagons the way squares do, so H3 only subdivides them approximately. Each cell ID encodes its place in the hierarchy, and you trade perfect containment for a grid where every neighbor is about the same distance away. The README does not go into the projection or indexing math, so the command-line tools are a way to poke at the behavior before reading further.

The Homebrew package installs small command-line wrappers around the C API. They let you convert a point to a cell and a cell back to geometry from a shell, with no code to write.
entry.install:
brew install h3
# Building from source instead needs a C compiler (gcc or clang), CMake, and Make. No accounts or API keys.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the H3 cell index for the Statue of Liberty at resolution 10. The README shows it as 8a2a1072b59ffff.
Prints the six corner vertices of that hexagon as latitude/longitude pairs.
Prints the hexagon's center coordinate, around 40.689, -74.044.

entry.whats_unique: It is a hexagonal grid with a hierarchy, and it openly accepts that subdivision across scales is only approximate. It also ships small shell tools so you can inspect cells without writing code.
entry.caveats: The homepage is thin marketing copy, and the README does not explain the extra tools like gridDisk or cellToLocalIj, so expect to read the documentation site for those.
